beats.text: A proof explains why a claim holds for every object meeting its assumptions. Four plus six equals ten is evidence for the even-plus-even claim, but testing examples can never cover all integers. We need a general reason.

Represent arbitrary even integers as two a and two b, where a and b are integers. Their sum factors as two times the integer a plus b. That matches the definition of even and completes a direct proof.

Mathematical induction uses a different structure: a starting case and a step that passes truth forward. For the sum of the first n positive integers, the claimed formula works at n equal to one, establishing the base case.

Assume the formula holds for a particular positive integer n, then add the next term. Factoring n plus one produces exactly the formula for n plus one. Combined with the base case, this implication establishes every positive integer case.

practice.prompt: Prove that the sum of two odd integers is even, using arbitrary integer variables.
practice.answer: Write the odd integers as 2a+1 and 2b+1. Their sum is 2(a+b+1), which is even because a+b+1 is an integer.

practice.prompt: Disprove the claim 'Every prime number is odd.' Explain why one example is sufficient here but not sufficient to prove a universal claim.
practice.answer: 2 is prime and even, so it contradicts the universal claim. A universal claim fails if even one allowed object violates it; finitely many positive examples do not establish all cases.

practice.prompt: Prove 1+3+…+(2n−1)=n² by induction. State both the base case and the induction step.
practice.answer: At n=1, 1=1². If the sum through 2n−1 is n², adding the next odd number 2n+1 gives n²+2n+1=(n+1)². Thus the claim holds for all positive integers.

takeaway: A proof uses general reasoning under stated assumptions; induction needs both a base case and a valid forward step.
scope: A direct parity proof, counterexamples, and one induction argument.
title: Proofs
objective: Build direct, contrapositive, contradiction, and induction arguments.
